claim: The intracellular signaling molecule Dishevelled (Dvl) mediates canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling via its PDZ domain.
source: The intracellular signaling molecule Dishevelled (Dvl) mediates canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling via its PDZ domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about Dvl function.

claim: The peptide-binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain can be occupied by Dvl's own highly conserved C-terminus, inducing a closed conformation.
source: Here we show that the peptide-binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain can be occupied by Dvl's own highly conserved C-terminus, inducing a closed conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through biophysical methods including NMR and ITC.

claim: In Xenopus, Wnt-regulated convergent extension (CE) is readily affected by Dvl mutants unable to form the closed conformation than by wild-type Dvl.
source: In Xenopus, Wnt-regulated convergent extension (CE) is readily affected by Dvl mutants unable to form the closed conformation than by wild-type Dvl.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Xenopus embryo experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: While Dvl cooperates with other Wnt pathway elements to activate canonical Wnt signaling, the open conformation of Dvl more effectively activates Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK).
source: We also demonstrate that while Dvl cooperates with other Wnt pathway elements to activate canonical Wnt signaling, the open conformation of Dvl more effectively activates Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK).
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase assays and western blots shown in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: The conformational change of Dvl regulates Wnt stimulated JNK activity in the non-canonical Wnt signaling.
source: These results suggest that together with other players in the Wnt signaling pathway, the conformational change of Dvl regulates Wnt stimulated JNK activity in the non-canonical Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling controls cell fate by regulating the cellular β-catenin level.
source: By regulating the cellular β-catenin level, canonical Wnt signaling controls cell fate, while non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a key role in controlling convergent extension (CE) and polarized cellular orientation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt signaling pathways cited from the literature.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a key role in controlling convergent extension (CE) and polarized cellular orientation.
source: By regulating the cellular β-catenin level, canonical Wnt signaling controls cell fate, while non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a key role in controlling convergent extension (CE) and polarized cellular orientation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt signaling pathways.

claim: Dishevelled (Dvl) is a key component of both canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling pathways.
source: Dishevelled (Dvl, or Dsh in Drosophila), a key component of both Wnt signaling pathways, relays Wnt signals downstream from the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Frizzled (Fz) (Noordermeer et al., 1994; Theisen et al., 1994; Axelrod et al., 1998; Wong et al., 2003; Park et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2006; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007; Simons et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Dvl relays Wnt signals downstream from the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Frizzled (Fz).
source: Dishevelled (Dvl, or Dsh in Drosophila), a key component of both Wnt signaling pathways, relays Wnt signals downstream from the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Frizzled (Fz) (Noordermeer et al., 1994; Theisen et al., 1994; Axelrod et al., 1998; Wong et al., 2003; Park et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2006; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007; Simons et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Dvl has been described as the 'policeman' at the intersection who directs different Wnt signals in different directions.
source: Therefore, Dvl has been described as the 'policeman' at the intersection who directs different Wnt signals in different directions (Boutros and Mlodzik, 1999).
evidence: This is a metaphorical description from the literature.

claim: Dvl contains highly conserved DIX, PDZ, and DEP domains and a highly conserved extreme C-terminus.
source: Dvl contains highly conserved DIX, PDZ, and DEP domains and a highly conserved extreme C-terminus (Figure 1) (Wharton, 2003; Wallingford and Habas, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PDZ and DIX domains are reported to be involved in canonical Wnt signaling.
source: The PDZ and DIX domains are reported to be involved in canonical Wnt signaling, while the PDZ and DEP domains play a crucial role in non-canonical Wnt signaling (Sokol et al., 1995; Axelrod et al., 1998; Boutros et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999; Moriguchi et al., 1999; Yamanaka et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: The PDZ and DEP domains play a crucial role in non-canonical Wnt signaling.
source: The PDZ and DIX domains are reported to be involved in canonical Wnt signaling, while the PDZ and DEP domains play a crucial role in non-canonical Wnt signaling (Sokol et al., 1995; Axelrod et al., 1998; Boutros et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999; Moriguchi et al., 1999; Yamanaka et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: The central PDZ domain participates in both canonical and non-canonical Wnt pathways.
source: The central PDZ domain not only participates in both pathways but also binds directly to the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Fz (Wong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The central PDZ domain binds directly to the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Fz.
source: The central PDZ domain not only participates in both pathways but also binds directly to the membrane-bound Wnt receptor Fz (Wong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Many Wnt signaling regulators mediate the different Wnt signaling pathways by interacting directly with the PDZ domain of Dvl.
source: Many Wnt signaling regulators have been reported to mediate the different Wnt signaling pathways by interacting directly with the PDZ domain of Dvl (Wharton, 2003; Wallingford and Habas, 2005; Gao and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: In most species the extreme C-terminus of Dvl resembles a class III PDZ-binding motif (E/D-X-Ф, where Ф represents hydrophobic residues such as F, I, L, M, or V).
source: Notably, in most species the extreme C-terminus of Dvl resembles a class III PDZ-binding motif (E/D-X-Ф, where Ф represents hydrophobic residues such as F, I, L, M, or V), while that of Dsh resembles a class II PDZ-binding motif (Ф-X-Ф) (Figure 1) (Tonikian et al., 2008; Lee and Zheng, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The extreme C-terminus of Dsh resembles a class II PDZ-binding motif (Ф-X-Ф).
source: Notably, in most species the extreme C-terminus of Dvl resembles a class III PDZ-binding motif (E/D-X-Ф, where Ф represents hydrophobic residues such as F, I, L, M, or V), while that of Dsh resembles a class II PDZ-binding motif (Ф-X-Ф) (Figure 1) (Tonikian et al., 2008; Lee and Zheng, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both Dvl-C and Dsh-C peptides competitively inhibited the interaction of Rox-DprC with the Dvl-1 PDZ domain.
source: Both Dvl-C and Dsh-C peptides competitively inhibited the interaction of Rox-DprC with the Dvl-1 PDZ domain (Figure 2), indicating that the three peptides competed for the same binding site on the PDZ domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The three peptides (Dvl-C, Dsh-C, and Rox-DprC) competed for the same binding site on the PDZ domain.
source: Both Dvl-C and Dsh-C peptides competitively inhibited the interaction of Rox-DprC with the Dvl-1 PDZ domain (Figure 2), indicating that the three peptides competed for the same binding site on the PDZ domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive inhibition data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inhibition constant (KI) for the Dvl-C peptide is 12.3 ± 7.8 μM.
source: The inhibition constants (KI) calculated from two independent experiments (12.3 ± 7.8 μM for the Dvl-C peptide and 26.8 ± 8.4 μM for the Dsh-C peptide) were similar to the binding affinity of Rox-DprC to the PDZ domain (KD ∼ 7.9 ± 0.9 μM) (Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The inhibition constant (KI) for the Dsh-C peptide is 26.8 ± 8.4 μM.
source: The inhibition constants (KI) calculated from two independent experiments (12.3 ± 7.8 μM for the Dvl-C peptide and 26.8 ± 8.4 μM for the Dsh-C peptide) were similar to the binding affinity of Rox-DprC to the PDZ domain (KD ∼ 7.9 ± 0.9 μM) (Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The binding affinity of Rox-DprC to the PDZ domain is KD ∼ 7.9 ± 0.9 μM.
source: The inhibition constants (KI) calculated from two independent experiments (12.3 ± 7.8 μM for the Dvl-C peptide and 26.8 ± 8.4 μM for the Dsh-C peptide) were similar to the binding affinity of Rox-DprC to the PDZ domain (KD ∼ 7.9 ± 0.9 μM) (Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is a measured value from previous studies cited.

claim: The binding affinity (KD) between Dvl-C and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain measured by ITC is 7.0 ± 0.7 μM.
source: We then measured the binding between Dvl-C and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) (Figure 3) and obtained a KD of 7.0 ± 0.7 μM, which is consistent with the KI value observed in the fluorescence study.
evidence: This is a measured value from ITC experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The KD value from ITC (7.0 ± 0.7 μM) is consistent with the KI value observed in the fluorescence study.
source: We then measured the binding between Dvl-C and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) (Figure 3) and obtained a KD of 7.0 ± 0.7 μM, which is consistent with the KI value observed in the fluorescence study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the two experimental methods.

claim: During titrations with Dvl-C and Dsh-C peptides, the NMR resonance of the residues in the PDZ domain's peptide binding site exhibited large chemical shift perturbations.
source: During these titrations, the NMR resonance of the residues in the PDZ domain's peptide binding site (Wong et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b) exhibited large chemical shift perturbations (Figure 4), further suggesting that both peptides interact with the Dvl PDZ domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both Dvl-C and Dsh-C peptides interact with the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: During these titrations, the NMR resonance of the residues in the PDZ domain's peptide binding site (Wong et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b) exhibited large chemical shift perturbations (Figure 4), further suggesting that both peptides interact with the Dvl PDZ domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: During the Dvl-C peptide titration, a few resonances of the PDZ domain disappeared and reappeared.
source: Moreover, during the Dvl-C peptide titration, a few resonances of the PDZ domain disappeared and reappeared (Figure 4), indicating that the Dvl-C peptide binds to the Dvl1 PDZ domain with higher binding affinity than the Dsh-C peptide does and that the complex is formed in the intermediate exchange range on the NMR time scale.
evidence: This is observed in the NMR experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Dvl-C peptide binds to the Dvl1 PDZ domain with higher binding affinity than the Dsh-C peptide does.
source: Moreover, during the Dvl-C peptide titration, a few resonances of the PDZ domain disappeared and reappeared (Figure 4), indicating that the Dvl-C peptide binds to the Dvl1 PDZ domain with higher binding affinity than the Dsh-C peptide does and that the complex is formed in the intermediate exchange range on the NMR time scale.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR resonance behavior during titration.

claim: The Dvl-C peptide/Dvl1 PDZ domain complex is formed in the intermediate exchange range on the NMR time scale.
source: Moreover, during the Dvl-C peptide titration, a few resonances of the PDZ domain disappeared and reappeared (Figure 4), indicating that the Dvl-C peptide binds to the Dvl1 PDZ domain with higher binding affinity than the Dsh-C peptide does and that the complex is formed in the intermediate exchange range on the NMR time scale.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR resonance behavior during titration.

claim: The Dvl PDZ domain contains six β-strands (βA∼βF) and two α-helix (αA and αB) structures.
source: The Dvl PDZ domain contains six β-strands (βA∼βF) and two α-helix (αA and αB) structures (Wong et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: This is structural information from previous studies cited.

claim: The Dvl-C peptide fits into the αB/βB peptide-binding groove of the Dvl PDZ domain and forms an additional β-strand with the αB-structure of the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: As expected, we found that the Dvl-C peptide fits into the αB/βB peptide-binding groove of the Dvl PDZ domain and forms an additional β-strand with the αB-structure of the Dvl PDZ domain (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is determined from the NMR solution structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: Six residues in the Dvl-C peptide participate in binding to the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: Nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE) data indicated that six residues in the Dvl-C peptide participate in binding (Figure 5—source data 1, 2).
evidence: This is determined from NOE data.

claim: The side chain of Met(0) in the Dvl-C peptide is located within a hydrophobic pocket formed by the side chains of residues Leu262, Ile264, and Ile266 in the βB-structure and residues Val325, Leu321, and Val318 in the αB-helix structure.
source: The side chain of Met(0) in the Dvl-C peptide is located within a hydrophobic pocket formed by the side chains of residues Leu262, Ile264, and Ile266 in the βB-structure and residues Val325, Leu321, and Val318 in the αB-helix structure (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is determined from the NMR solution structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: The side chain of residue Asp(-2) in the Dvl-C peptide forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of residue Arg322 in the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: Notably, the side chain of residue Asp(-2) in the Dvl-C peptide forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of residue Arg322 in the Dvl PDZ domain (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is determined from the NMR solution structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Arg322Ala substitution dramatically weakened the binding of Dvl PDZ to the Dvl-C peptide.
source: Consistent with this finding, the Arg322Ala substitution dramatically weakened the binding of Dvl PDZ to the Dvl-C peptide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Lee et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR titration experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The side chains of two hydrophobic Dvl-C residues, Val(-3) and Phe(-5), interact with the side chains of the Val318 and Ile266 residues in the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: The side chains of two hydrophobic Dvl-C residues, Val(-3) and Phe(-5), interact with the side chains of the Val318 and Ile266 residues in the Dvl PDZ domain (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is determined from the NMR solution structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: Little polarization change was observed when mC1 proteins were added to Rox-DprC solution.
source: Little polarization change was observed when mC1 proteins were added to Rox-DprC solution, whereas large polarization changes were induced by adding mC1-CΔ7 (Figure 6), indicating that the binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain was occupied by its intrinsic C-terminus in the mC1 construct.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Large polarization changes were induced by adding mC1-CΔ7 to Rox-DprC solution.
source: Little polarization change was observed when mC1 proteins were added to Rox-DprC solution, whereas large polarization changes were induced by adding mC1-CΔ7 (Figure 6), indicating that the binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain was occupied by its intrinsic C-terminus in the mC1 construct.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain was occupied by its intrinsic C-terminus in the mC1 construct.
source: Little polarization change was observed when mC1 proteins were added to Rox-DprC solution, whereas large polarization changes were induced by adding mC1-CΔ7 (Figure 6), indicating that the binding pocket of the Dvl PDZ domain was occupied by its intrinsic C-terminus in the mC1 construct.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The binding affinity between Rox-DprC and mC1-CΔ7 is 3.7 ± 0.5 μM.
source: The binding affinity between Rox-DprC and mC1-CΔ7 was 3.7 ± 0.5 μM, closely approximating the affinity between Rox-DprC and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain.
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The binding affinity between Rox-DprC and mC1-CΔ7 closely approximates the affinity between Rox-DprC and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain.
source: The binding affinity between Rox-DprC and mC1-CΔ7 was 3.7 ± 0.5 μM, closely approximating the affinity between Rox-DprC and the Dvl-1 PDZ domain.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the measured binding affinities.

claim: The estimated binding affinity between Rox-DrpC and mD1 is greater than 70 μM.
source: In contrast, the estimated binding affinity between Rox-DrpC and mD1 was greater than 70 μM, suggesting not only that the Dvl PDZ domain binds intrinsically to the Dvl C-terminus but also that this binding interferes with interactions between the Dvl PDZ domain and its other binding partners in the Wnt signaling pathways.
evidence: This is an estimated value from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The intrinsic binding of the Dvl PDZ domain to the Dvl C-terminus interferes with interactions between the Dvl PDZ domain and its other binding partners in the Wnt signaling pathways.
source: In contrast, the estimated binding affinity between Rox-DrpC and mD1 was greater than 70 μM, suggesting not only that the Dvl PDZ domain binds intrinsically to the Dvl C-terminus but also that this binding interferes with interactions between the Dvl PDZ domain and its other binding partners in the Wnt signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding affinity data.

claim: At low and intermediate doses, neither XDsh nor XDsh-CΔ8 substantially affected canonical Wnt signaling.
source: At low and intermediate doses, neither XDsh nor XDsh-CΔ8 substantially affected canonical Wnt signaling (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from luciferase assays.

claim: At high dose (500 pg), both XDsh and XDsh-CΔ8 enhanced canonical Wnt signaling, but wild-type XDsh was a stronger activator.
source: At the high dose, both constructs enhanced canonical Wnt signaling, but wild-type XDsh was a stronger activator (Figure 7), consistent with a previous report showing involvement of the extreme C-terminal region of Dvl in activation of canonical Wnt signaling (Tauriello et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: The extreme C-terminal region of Dvl is involved in activation of canonical Wnt signaling.
source: At the high dose, both constructs enhanced canonical Wnt signaling, but wild-type XDsh was a stronger activator (Figure 7), consistent with a previous report showing involvement of the extreme C-terminal region of Dvl in activation of canonical Wnt signaling (Tauriello et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation from the literature.

claim: At all three doses (80 pg, 200 pg, and 500 pg), XDsh-CΔ8 mRNA caused greater body axis shortening and dorsal tail flexion than did wild-type XDsh.
source: At all three doses (80 pg, 200 pg, and 500 pg), XDsh-CΔ8 mRNA caused greater body axis shortening and dorsal tail flexion than did wild-type XDsh (Figure 8A), suggesting that XDsh-CΔ8 is more active than wild-type XDsh in inducing the CE phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Xenopus embryo experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: XDsh-CΔ8 is more active than wild-type XDsh in inducing the CE phenotype.
source: At all three doses (80 pg, 200 pg, and 500 pg), XDsh-CΔ8 mRNA caused greater body axis shortening and dorsal tail flexion than did wild-type XDsh (Figure 8A), suggesting that XDsh-CΔ8 is more active than wild-type XDsh in inducing the CE phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the Xenopus embryo phenotype data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The phenotypes were very similar after injection of XDsh-CΔ8 and after injection of Xdd1.
source: We injected equal quantities (500 pg) of N-terminal myc-tagged Xdd1, XDsh-CΔ8, and wild-type XDsh mRNA, respectively, into the dorsal blastomeres of 4-cell Xenopus embryos and found that the phenotypes were very similar after injection of XDsh-CΔ8 and after injection of Xdd1 (Figure 8B), suggesting that the 'open' Dvl is more active than the 'closed' wild-type Dvl in inducing the Xenopus CE phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Xenopus embryo experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The 'open' Dvl is more active than the 'closed' wild-type Dvl in inducing the Xenopus CE phenotype.
source: We injected equal quantities (500 pg) of N-terminal myc-tagged Xdd1, XDsh-CΔ8, and wild-type XDsh mRNA, respectively, into the dorsal blastomeres of 4-cell Xenopus embryos and found that the phenotypes were very similar after injection of XDsh-CΔ8 and after injection of Xdd1 (Figure 8B), suggesting that the 'open' Dvl is more active than the 'closed' wild-type Dvl in inducing the Xenopus CE phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the Xenopus embryo phenotype data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: JNK regulates CE through non-canonical Wnt-PCP signaling in Xenopus embryos.
source: In Xenopus embryos, JNK is known to regulate CE through non-canonical Wnt-PCP signaling (Sokol, 1996, 2000; Jones and Chen, 2007), and either hyperactivation or JNK depletion dysregulates CE (Yamanaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Either hyperactivation or JNK depletion dysregulates CE.
source: In Xenopus embryos, JNK is known to regulate CE through non-canonical Wnt-PCP signaling (Sokol, 1996, 2000; Jones and Chen, 2007), and either hyperactivation or JNK depletion dysregulates CE (Yamanaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation from the literature.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type XDsh induced slightly greater JNK phosphorylation than observed in uninjected control cells.
source: Overexpression of wild-type XDsh induced slightly greater JNK phosphorylation than observed in uninjected control cells. However, both Xdd1 and XDsh-CΔ8 induced JNK phosphorylation more potently (Figure 9A), suggesting that deletion of the XDsh C-terminal region renders XDsh more active in the non-canonical Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Both Xdd1 and XDsh-CΔ8 induced JNK phosphorylation more potently than wild-type XDsh.
source: Overexpression of wild-type XDsh induced slightly greater JNK phosphorylation than observed in uninjected control cells. However, both Xdd1 and XDsh-CΔ8 induced JNK phosphorylation more potently (Figure 9A), suggesting that deletion of the XDsh C-terminal region renders XDsh more active in the non-canonical Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Deletion of the XDsh C-terminal region renders XDsh more active in the non-canonical Wnt pathway.
source: Overexpression of wild-type XDsh induced slightly greater JNK phosphorylation than observed in uninjected control cells. However, both Xdd1 and XDsh-CΔ8 induced JNK phosphorylation more potently (Figure 9A), suggesting that deletion of the XDsh C-terminal region renders XDsh more active in the non-canonical Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the JNK phosphorylation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mutant Dvl lacking the PDZ domain activates JNK more effectively in COS-7 cells than wild-type Dvl.
source: This finding is consistent with an early report of more effective JNK activation in COS-7 cells expressing mutant Dvl lacking the PDZ domain than in cells expressing wild-type Dvl (Sokol et al., 1995; Axelrod et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999; Moriguchi et al., 1999; Yamanaka et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: XDsh-CΔ8 activated AP1-luciferase activity more strongly than wild-type XDsh.
source: When equal quantities (500 pg) of XDsh-CΔ8 or wild-type XDsh mRNA were injected into the dorsal region of 4-cell Xenopus embryos and luciferase activity was assayed at the late gastrula stage, XDsh-CΔ8 clearly activated AP1-luciferase activity more strongly (Figure 9B), indicating that Dvl in the open conformation activates JNK more potently than Dvl in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP1-luciferase assays shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Dvl in the open conformation activates JNK more potently than Dvl in the closed conformation.
source: When equal quantities (500 pg) of XDsh-CΔ8 or wild-type XDsh mRNA were injected into the dorsal region of 4-cell Xenopus embryos and luciferase activity was assayed at the late gastrula stage, XDsh-CΔ8 clearly activated AP1-luciferase activity more strongly (Figure 9B), indicating that Dvl in the open conformation activates JNK more potently than Dvl in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the AP1-luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In Xenopus, both activation and inhibition of non-canonical Wnt signaling result in planar cell polarity (PCP) defects and produce CE phenotype.
source: In Xenopus, both activation and inhibition of non-canonical Wnt signaling result in planar cell polarity (PCP) defects and produce CE phenotype (Djiane et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation from the literature.

claim: XDsh-CΔ8 and Xdd1 strongly inhibited the activin-induced elongation of ectodermal explants (CE outcomes) as compared to controls.
source: As expected, XDsh-CΔ8 and the dominant-negative mutant Xdd1 strongly inhibited the activin-induced elongation of ectodermal explants (CE outcomes) as compared to controls, while wild-type XDsh had little effect (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ectodermal explant experiments shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: Wild-type XDsh had little effect on activin-induced elongation of ectodermal explants.
source: As expected, XDsh-CΔ8 and the dominant-negative mutant Xdd1 strongly inhibited the activin-induced elongation of ectodermal explants (CE outcomes) as compared to controls, while wild-type XDsh had little effect (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ectodermal explant experiments shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: Co-expression of a dominant-negative JNK mutant (dnJNK) with XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 efficiently rescued explant elongation.
source: However, co-expression of a dominant-negative JNK mutant (dnJNK), which inhibits non-canonical Wnt signaling (Yamanaka et al., 2002; Carron et al., 2005), with XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 efficiently rescued explant elongation (Figure 9G,H), indicating that the CE defects induced by XDsh-CΔ8 and Xdd1 are the result of JNK activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ectodermal explant experiments shown in Figure 9G-H.

claim: The CE defects induced by XDsh-CΔ8 and Xdd1 are the result of JNK activation.
source: However, co-expression of a dominant-negative JNK mutant (dnJNK), which inhibits non-canonical Wnt signaling (Yamanaka et al., 2002; Carron et al., 2005), with XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 efficiently rescued explant elongation (Figure 9G,H), indicating that the CE defects induced by XDsh-CΔ8 and Xdd1 are the result of JNK activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 9G-H.

claim: dnJNK inhibits non-canonical Wnt signaling.
source: However, co-expression of a dominant-negative JNK mutant (dnJNK), which inhibits non-canonical Wnt signaling (Yamanaka et al., 2002; Carron et al., 2005), with XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 efficiently rescued explant elongation (Figure 9G,H), indicating that the CE defects induced by XDsh-CΔ8 and Xdd1 are the result of JNK activation.
evidence: This is supported by citations from the literature.

claim: The abnormal CE phenotype was substantially rescued when the embryos were coinjected with dnJNK.
source: Injection of XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 alone resulted in embryos with short and bent axis, reflecting CE defects. However, the abnormal CE phenotype was substantially rescued when the embryos were coinjected with dnJNK (Figure 9I), suggesting that JNK activation induced by the Dvl open conformation (i.e., use of XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1) had resulted in the CE phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole embryo experiments shown in Figure 9I.

claim: JNK activation induced by the Dvl open conformation results in the CE phenotype.
source: Injection of XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1 alone resulted in embryos with short and bent axis, reflecting CE defects. However, the abnormal CE phenotype was substantially rescued when the embryos were coinjected with dnJNK (Figure 9I), suggesting that JNK activation induced by the Dvl open conformation (i.e., use of XDsh-CΔ8 or Xdd1) had resulted in the CE phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 9I.

claim: Many Wnt signaling regulators directly bind to and inhibit the Dvl PDZ domain.
source: Many Wnt signaling regulators directly bind to and inhibit the Dvl PDZ domain (Wharton, 2003; Wallingford and Habas, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations from the literature.

claim: A series of small-molecule inhibitors were developed that disrupt Fz–Dvl interaction.
source: To block Wnt signaling transduction at the Dvl level, we also developed a series of small-molecule inhibitors that disrupt Fz–Dvl interaction (Shan et al., 2005, 2012; Grandy et al., 2009; Shan and Zheng, 2009; Lee et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the authors' previous work.

claim: All of the Wnt-regulating proteins and small molecule inhibitors target the site on the surface of the Dvl PDZ domain that binds to the molecule's own C-terminus.
source: Because all of the Wnt-regulating proteins and small molecule inhibitors target the site on the surface of the Dvl PDZ domain that binds to the molecule's own C-terminus, these agents should release the Dvl C-terminus from its intramolecular binding and open the closed conformation of Dvl.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and binding data.

claim: Wnt-regulating proteins and small molecule inhibitors should release the Dvl C-terminus from its intramolecular binding and open the closed conformation of Dvl.
source: Because all of the Wnt-regulating proteins and small molecule inhibitors target the site on the surface of the Dvl PDZ domain that binds to the molecule's own C-terminus, these agents should release the Dvl C-terminus from its intramolecular binding and open the closed conformation of Dvl.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the competitive binding mechanism.

claim: The small molecule 3289–8625 penetrates the Xenopus embryo and binds to the PDZ domain of Dvl.
